ch46.note: The sanjikkoku-bune, the long, low passenger boats that plied the Yodo River between Fushimi and Osaka’s Hachikenya landing, rated at a nominal thirty koku of cargo (see the note on koku at chapter 2). They were the ordinary public transport of the route, and here they carry the Shinsengumi’s wounded down from the lost battle.

ch46.anchor: a fortress of metal walls and boiling moats
ch46.note: This renders kinjō-tōchi, a Chinese-derived phrase (“walls of metal, a moat of boiling water”) for an impregnable stronghold. Osaka Castle, raised by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the 1580s and rebuilt on a vaster scale by the Tokugawa after 1620, was the greatest fortress in the land, sited by the shogunate expressly to hold the western daimyo in check. That Yoshinobu would abandon it without a fight — the subject of the rest of this chapter — is precisely what made his flight so stunning.

ch46.anchor: the Winter and Summer sieges of Osaka
ch46.note: In the winter of 1614 and the summer of 1615 Tokugawa Ieyasu twice besieged Osaka Castle to destroy the Toyotomi house that Hideyoshi had left behind; the castle fell and the Toyotomi were annihilated, sealing Tokugawa supremacy. Sanada Yukimura (Nobushige), the defenders’ most brilliant captain, was killed in the final battle and became the type of the doomed loyal warrior. Shiba’s irony is exact: Toshizō now looks to the same castle for a last stand, but with the sides reversed — it is the Tokugawa cause that is failing.

Inoue Kaoru (1836–1915), known in his Chōshū youth as Inoue Monta; one of the “Chōshū Five” who studied secretly in London. He rose to be a leading Meiji statesman — foreign minister and, as Shiba’s aside notes, a marquis. His analysis quoted here, of how the shogunate might have strangled the thinly-held Imperial position from Osaka, is the counsel of a man who became one of the age’s shrewdest political operators.

ch46.anchor: toward ten at night on the sixth of the First Month
ch46.note: Yoshinobu’s secret flight from Osaka Castle on the night of Keiō 4/1/6 (30 January 1868) is historical fact and the decisive act of the Boshin War’s opening. Abandoning an intact army and an impregnable fortress, he slipped out with a small party — among them Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu and, as the next paragraph notes, Katamori’s brother Matsudaira Sadaaki of Kuwana — boarded an American warship (the USS Iroquois) for the night off Tenpōzan, and at dawn transferred to the shogunal steam warship Kaiyō-maru, which bore him to Edo. His own commanders were not told. With this, the shogunal cause collapsed not in battle but by the desertion of its head.

ch46.anchor: He has left a written account of it
ch46.note: Fukuchi Gen’ichirō, pen-name Ōchi (1841–1906), a shogunal interpreter present in the castle that night who became one of Meiji Japan’s foremost journalists (editor of the Tōkyō Nichi Nichi Shimbun) and a Kabuki playwright. The passage that follows is Shiba’s condensation of Fukuchi’s memoir; the “I” of it is Fukuchi himself.

Enomoto Takeaki (1836–1908), the Dutch-trained commander of the shogunal navy and captain of the Kaiyō-maru, the finest warship in Japanese waters. He refused to surrender the fleet after Edo’s fall, carried the remnant of the Tokugawa forces north, and set up the short-lived republic at Hakodate where this novel will end; pardoned afterward, he became a Meiji cabinet minister. He enters the story here, at the edge of Yoshinobu’s flight, as the man who still commands the ships off Tenpōzan.
